text: Scholars continue to debate the extent to which the Gospel narratives reflect historical events versus theological construction. The quest for the historical Jesus has proceeded through several distinct phases, each with its own methodological assumptions.

The meaning of Jesus’s baptism has been interpreted in various ways. Some scholars emphasise its connection to Jewish purification rites; others see it as Jesus’s identification with sinful humanity; a third view interprets it as Jesus’s anointing for his messianic mission.

The significance of the empty tomb narrative is disputed among New Testament scholars. For some, it constitutes the earliest evidence for the resurrection; for others, it represents a later apologetic development designed to counter claims that Jesus’s body was simply missing.

N. T. Wright argues that the resurrection must be understood within its first-century Jewish context, where ‘resurrection’ meant bodily re-embodiment rather than spiritual survival. By contrast, John Dominic Crossan contends that the original Christian proclamation did not depend on an empty tomb.

The criterion of dissimilarity has been a foundational tool in historical Jesus research since Ernst Käsemann’s 1953 lecture. It holds that material which cannot be derived from either early Judaism or the early church may be attributed to Jesus himself.

The relationship between John’s Gospel and the Synoptics remains a central problem in New Testament studies. P. Gardner-Smith’s 1938 argument for John’s independence from the Synoptics gained wide acceptance, though scholars such as C. K. Barrett and more recently Richard Bauckham have challenged this consensus.

The parables of Jesus have been analysed through a variety of hermeneutical lenses. Adolf Jülicher’s rejection of allegorical interpretation in the late 19th century established the modern approach, while C. H. Dodd and Joachim Jeremias emphasised their eschatological setting. More recent scholarship has drawn on literary and social-scientific methodologies.

E. P. Sanders’s 1977 book Paul and Palestinian Judaism reshaped scholarly understanding of first-century Judaism. Sanders argued that Judaism was not a religion of works-righteousness but of ‘covenantal nomism,’ in which obedience to the law was a response to God’s grace rather than a means of earning it.

The Christological titles used in the New Testament — Son of Man, Son of God, Christ, Lord — have been the subject of extensive analysis. Oscar Cullmann’s The Christology of the New Testament remains influential, though more recent works have questioned his sharp distinction between functional and ontological Christology.

The problem of the Synoptic relationships, known as the Synoptic Problem, has generated several major hypotheses. The Two-Source Hypothesis, which posits Marcan priority and the existence of a sayings source Q, remains the dominant view, though the Farrer Hypothesis (Markan priority without Q) and the Griesbach Hypothesis (Matthean priority) retain significant scholarly support.

The significance of the Kingdom of God in Jesus’s teaching has been interpreted along several lines. C. H. Dodd’s ‘realised eschatology’ held that the Kingdom had already arrived in Jesus’s ministry; Albert Schweitzer’s ‘thoroughgoing eschatology’ saw it as entirely future; the majority view today is some form of ‘inaugurated eschatology.’

Scholarly assessments of the historical reliability of Acts range widely. The traditional view, represented by F. F. Bruce and more recently by Colin Hemer, treats Luke as a careful historian. A more sceptical tradition, following Ernst Haenchen, views Acts as primarily a theological narrative with limited historical value.

The development of early Christology has been a major focus of research since Wilhelm Bousset’s Kyrios Christos (1913). Scholars have debated whether the highest Christological titles originated in Palestinian Jewish Christianity or later Hellenistic communities, and whether the worship of Jesus represented a break with Jewish monotheism.

The Jesus Seminar, founded by Robert Funk in 1985, employed a distinctive voting methodology to assess the authenticity of Gospel sayings. Its conclusions — that only about 18% of the sayings attributed to Jesus are likely authentic — have been sharply criticised by scholars such as Luke Timothy Johnson and N. T. Wright.

The question of Paul’s relationship to Judaism has undergone a substantial reassessment since the publication of E. P. Sanders’s work. The so-called ‘New Perspective on Paul,’ advanced by James D. G. Dunn and N. T. Wright, argues that Paul’s critiques were directed not at Jewish legalism but at the exclusion of Gentiles from the covenant community.

Literary approaches to the Gospels have gained prominence alongside traditional historical-critical methods. Narrative criticism examines the finished text as a coherent story, analysing elements such as plot, characterisation, and rhetorical devices without attempting to reconstruct the text’s prehistory.

The role of women in the early Christian movement has been the subject of significant feminist and social-historical scholarship. Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza’s In Memory of Her (1983) argued that women held leadership roles in the Jesus movement that were subsequently suppressed in the emerging institutional church.

The question of whether Jesus claimed to be divine has been one of the most contentious issues in historical Jesus research. While the Fourth Gospel presents explicit claims, the Synoptics are more ambiguous, leading to competing interpretations about the development of early Christology.

The use of form criticism in Gospel studies, pioneered by Martin Dibelius and Rudolf Bultmann in the early twentieth century, sought to classify individual Gospel units according to their literary form and reconstruct the oral traditions behind them. The method has since been critiqued for its assumptions about oral transmission and its neglect of the evangelists’ own literary activity.

Albert Schweitzer’s The Quest of the Historical Jesus (1906) argued that nineteenth-century liberal lives of Jesus had simply projected their own ideals onto him. Schweitzer’s portrait of Jesus as an apocalyptic prophet who expected the imminent end of the world set the agenda for much twentieth-century research.

The criterion of embarrassment suggests that the baptism of Jesus by John is likely historical, since it is improbable the early church would have invented an episode in which Jesus appears subordinate to John. The theological discomfort this pericope caused is evident in Matthew’s insertion of John’s protest.

Matthew’s addition of the formula quotation ‘out of Egypt I have called my son’ reflects his community’s concern with presenting Jesus as the fulfilment of Israel’s story. By shaping the infancy narrative around the Exodus typology, Matthew constructs a Christology in which Jesus recapitulates the history of the people of God.

Luke alters Mark’s portrait of the disciples in order to present them as more faithful and worthy successors to Jesus’s mission. Where Mark emphasises their failure and incomprehension, Luke consistently softens these elements, probably reflecting his concern with legitimating the apostolic leadership of his own time.

The theological significance of the transfiguration has been variously understood. Christologically, the passage asserts Jesus’s superiority to Moses and Elijah, the twin pillars of the law and the prophets. The divine voice’s command to ‘listen to him’ may reflect the early community’s conviction that Jesus’s teaching now supersedes the Mosaic Torah.

By relocating the cleansing of the Temple from the end of his Gospel to the beginning, John presents Jesus’s entire ministry as a challenge to the Temple establishment. This redactional move probably indicates that for the Johannine community, the replacement of the Temple by Jesus’s own body was not an afterthought but the programme of his mission from the outset.

The parable of the Good Samaritan is best understood as a challenge to the hearer’s construction of social identity. By making a Samaritan the exemplary neighbour, Jesus subverts the honour-shame dynamics of first-century Judaean society, in which ethnic boundaries determined moral obligations. The parable does not merely illustrate love of neighbour; it redefines who counts as a neighbour.

Scholars remain divided on whether the Fourth Gospel reflects a high Christology that developed gradually within the Johannine community or whether it preserves an independent early tradition of exalted claims about Jesus. The Gospel’s distinctive ‘I am’ sayings, with their allusions to the divine name, could suggest an early binitarian devotional pattern rather than a late doctrinal development.

The criterion of multiple attestation supports the historicity of Jesus’s table fellowship with tax collectors and sinners. This motif appears independently in Mark, Q, and uniquely Lukan material, and it coheres with the early church’s own struggles over table fellowship with Gentiles, which they would have been unlikely to fabricate as a precedent for a practice that remained controversial.

Raymond Brown’s analysis of the infancy narratives demonstrated that Matthew and Luke drew on independent traditions structured around different theological concerns. Matthew emphasises Joseph’s role and the fulfilment of prophecy; Luke foregrounds Mary and the motif of the lowly being exalted. These differences are best explained by the evangelists’ distinct Christological and ecclesiological interests.

Applying a postcolonial reading of Mark’s Gospel reveals the extent to which the narrative is shaped by the politics of Roman occupation. The Gerasene demoniac, named ‘Legion,’ may represent a coded critique of Roman military power, while the passion narrative can be read as an exposure of imperial violence masquerading as justice.

Through a feminist hermeneutical lens, the story of the woman with the haemorrhage reveals both the agency of a marginalised figure and the subversive character of Jesus’s healing ministry. By touching Jesus, she transgresses purity boundaries; by publicly commending her faith, Jesus restores not only her health but her place in the community.

Using social-scientific models of honour and shame, the controversy stories in the Gospels can be understood as public contests in which Jesus and his opponents engage in a form of social challenge-and-riposte. Jesus’s ability to deflect hostile questions and turn them back on his interrogators would have been perceived by ancient audiences as demonstrations of honour won in verbal combat.

Employing reader-response criticism, one may observe that Mark’s abrupt ending at 16:8 places the burden of interpretation on the audience. The women’s fear and silence at the tomb forces the reader to decide whether the promise of resurrection is fulfilled, thereby implicating the reader in the proclamation that the characters in the narrative fail to deliver.

Drawing on memory theory, recent scholarship has proposed that the Gospels reflect not a direct transcription of events but the remembered Jesus as mediated through communal recollection, liturgical practice, and catechetical needs. The variations among parallel accounts may thus represent the flexible and constructive character of social memory rather than literary dependence alone.

The Johannine prologue’s identification of Jesus as the Logos has been interpreted against the background of both Jewish Wisdom traditions and Hellenistic philosophy. It is plausible that the evangelist deliberately employed a term that resonated in both contexts, presenting Jesus as the fulfilment of the Wisdom that Jews already associated with Torah and the rational principle that Greeks understood as the ordering force of the cosmos.

The consensus view that the Synoptic Gospels were written after 70 CE has been challenged by scholars who argue that the absence of any explicit reference to the Temple’s destruction as a past event is more naturally explained by a pre-70 date. However, the majority of scholars regard the Olivet Discourse’s detailed predictions as vaticinia ex eventu, composed with knowledge of the Roman siege.

The concept of realised eschatology in the Fourth Gospel represents a distinctive development in early Christian thought. Whereas the Synoptics preserve a tension between present and future dimensions of the Kingdom, John appears to have collapsed the future into the present: eternal life, judgement, and resurrection are already experienced through belief in Jesus.

Paul’s language of being ‘in Christ’ has been analysed as an expression of participatory soteriology. Rather than framing salvation primarily in forensic terms as a declaration of righteousness, this motif suggests that Paul conceived of salvation as incorporation into Christ’s own death and resurrection, effecting a transformation of the believer’s very mode of existence.

The Pastoral Epistles’ concern with sound doctrine and established church offices probably reflects a later stage of community formation than the undisputed Pauline letters. The emphasis on episkopoi and presbyteroi suggests a process of institutionalisation that was under way by the end of the first century, as charismatic leadership gave way to structured authority.

The Apocalypse of John employs a dense symbolic vocabulary drawn from Jewish apocalyptic tradition, but its meaning for its original audience must be reconstructed from the political and social situation of the Asian churches. The beast from the sea, with its echoes of Daniel’s visions, probably represents Roman imperial power, while the mark of the beast may allude to the imperial cult’s penetration of economic life.

Ignatius of Antioch’s letters reveal an early second-century bishop articulating a theology of unity centred on the monepiscopate. His insistence that nothing be done without the bishop may reflect not an established reality but an aspirational programme, suggesting that his own authority was contested and that the threefold ministry was still being consolidated.

The Didache’s eucharistic prayers, which make no explicit reference to the Last Supper or the words of institution, have prompted debate about the diversity of early Christian liturgical practice. It may be that the Didache preserves a form of meal tradition from Jewish Christian communities that had not yet integrated the Pauline and Synoptic institution narratives into their worship.

Justin Martyr’s doctrine of the Logos spermatikos represents an early attempt to reconcile Christian faith with Greek philosophy. By arguing that Socrates and other pre-Christian philosophers participated in the Logos, Justin could affirm the truth of Greek thought while asserting its subordination to the full revelation in Christ. This strategy of appropriation and subordination would prove influential in subsequent patristic theology.

Irenaeus’s Adversus Haereses constructs orthodoxy partly through the representation and refutation of its others. His characterisation of Gnostic systems as incoherent and morally dangerous is not merely descriptive but rhetorical, serving to establish the boundaries of acceptable Christian identity at a time when those boundaries were still permeable.

The criterion of coherence suggests that Jesus’s proclamation of the Kingdom of God was intimately connected with his practice of healing and exorcism. If the Kingdom meant the overthrow of satanic power, then exorcisms were not merely benevolent acts but performative demonstrations that the eschatological reign of God was already breaking into the present age.

The trial of Jesus before the Sanhedrin, as narrated in Mark and Matthew, presents numerous historical difficulties. The nocturnal gathering, the apparent violation of Mishnaic procedural rules, and the unanimity of the verdict may indicate that the evangelists have shaped the narrative to emphasise Jewish responsibility, reflecting the growing estrangement between church and synagogue at the time of composition.

The Gospel of Thomas, discovered at Nag Hammadi in 1945, has been the subject of vigorous debate regarding its relationship to the canonical tradition. Some scholars, notably those associated with the Jesus Seminar, have argued that Thomas preserves independent and possibly early sayings of Jesus; others maintain that it represents a secondary gnosticising redaction of Synoptic material.

The significance of the Son of Man sayings in the Gospels has generated extensive scholarly literature. The sayings fall into three categories — earthly activity, suffering and vindication, and future coming — and their authenticity and reference have been disputed. The fact that ‘Son of Man’ is never used as a confessional title in the epistles suggests it was a distinctive feature of Jesus’s own idiom that the early church did not adopt for its own Christological proclamation.

Mark’s so-called ‘messianic secret’ — Jesus’s repeated commands to silence — was identified by William Wrede as a theological motif rather than a historical recollection. Wrede argued that Mark retrojected the post-resurrection recognition of Jesus’s messiahship back into the pre-Easter narrative, explaining why Jesus was not recognised as Messiah during his lifetime as a matter of his own concealment.

The household codes of Colossians and Ephesians have been read as evidence of the early church’s accommodation to Greco-Roman social norms. Whereas the Pauline epistles contain more egalitarian impulses, the Haustafeln appear to reinforce patriarchal structures. Feminist critics have argued that this trajectory represents a progressive loss of the radical social vision of the earliest Jesus movement.

The Corinthian correspondence reveals a community struggling with social stratification in its common meal. Paul’s rebuke of those who eat before others indicates that the Lord’s Supper was not yet a token ritual but a genuine meal, and that economic inequalities within the congregation were being reproduced in its central act of worship. This would have scandalised Paul’s conviction that in Christ, social distinctions were abolished.

Scholarly assessments of the authentic Pauline corpus have been generally stable, with seven letters — Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon — widely accepted as genuine. The disputed letters, particularly the Pastorals, exhibit differences in vocabulary, theological emphasis, and ecclesiastical structure that most scholars regard as indications of pseudonymous authorship in a later generation.

The phrase ‘the faith of Jesus Christ’ (pistis Christou) in Paul has been the subject of an important grammatical and theological debate. The objective genitive reading (‘faith in Christ’) dominated traditional interpretation, but a growing number of scholars argue for a subjective genitive (‘the faithfulness of Christ’), which would shift the emphasis from human belief to Christ’s own obedient faith as the basis of justification.

The delay of the parousia posed a significant theological challenge for the early church, and traces of this crisis can be detected within the New Testament itself. The shift from Paul’s early expectation of an imminent return to Luke’s extended salvation-historical scheme, and finally to 2 Peter’s explicit defence of the delay, documents the community’s struggle to maintain eschatological hope in changing circumstances.

The Lukan travel narrative (9:51–19:27) has long been recognised as a distinctive compositional unit. Its length and the density of uniquely Lukan material within it suggest that Luke has gathered traditions for which he could find no place in the Markan framework, creating a journey toward Jerusalem that serves as the narrative context for Jesus’s teaching on discipleship and the coming Kingdom.

The question of the historical Jesus’s self-understanding remains one of the most elusive problems in New Testament scholarship. Did Jesus regard himself as the Messiah, the Son of Man, a prophet, or simply a teacher of wisdom? The answer depends heavily on methodological decisions about which Gospel material is accepted as authentic and how that material is configured into a coherent portrait.

The Matthean community appears to have been engaged in an intramural debate with formative Judaism over the interpretation of Torah. Matthew’s Jesus upholds the Law while radicalising its demands and asserting his own interpretive authority. This suggests a community that had not yet separated from the synagogue but was in the process of defining its identity over against the emerging rabbinic movement.

The role of apocalyptic in Jesus’s teaching continues to divide scholars. Those who follow Schweitzer’s thoroughgoing eschatology regard apocalyptic expectation as central; others, such as those associated with the North American Jesus Seminar, treat the apocalyptic sayings as secondary additions by the early church. A mediating position holds that Jesus proclaimed an eschatological Kingdom but not in the temporally specific terms that some Synoptic passages suggest.

Galatians 3:28 — ‘there is no longer Jew or Greek, slave or free, male and female’ — has been called the Magna Carta of Christian egalitarianism. The formula probably originated in a baptismal context and represents Paul’s conviction that the old creation distinctions were relativised by incorporation into Christ. The extent to which this theological insight translated into social practice remains sharply debated.

The Apocalypse of Peter, though eventually excluded from the canon, provides important evidence for the diversity of early Christian eschatological imagination. Its graphic depictions of post-mortem punishments, graded according to specific sins, reflect the influence of Jewish apocalyptic tours of hell and anticipate the elaborate vision of the afterlife that would characterise mediaeval Christianity.

The Shepherd of Hermas, widely read in the second-century church and nearly included in the canon, offers a window into the practical piety and penitential discipline of Roman Christianity. Its teaching on post-baptismal repentance represents a relaxation of the stricter position attested in Hebrews, responding to the pastoral crisis created when members of the community sinned after baptism.

The Christological controversy of the fourth century, culminating in the Council of Nicaea, had deep roots in the diverse interpretations of Jesus’s relationship to God already present in the New Testament. The subordinationist tendencies visible in the Synoptics, the high Christology of John, and the pre-existence theology of the Pauline and deutero-Pauline letters provided the raw materials from which later doctrinal formulations were constructed.

The designation of Jesus as ‘prophet’ in the Gospels and Acts may preserve an early Christological category that was subsequently eclipsed by higher titles. The crowds’ acclamation of Jesus as ‘the prophet from Nazareth’ and the Emmaus disciples’ description of him as ‘a prophet mighty in deed and word’ suggest that the prophetic model was an important component of early Christian proclamation, though it proved insufficient for expressing the full significance the church attributed to Jesus.

The Fourth Gospel’s portrait of ‘the Jews’ (hoi Ioudaioi) as Jesus’s opponents has been a source of intense scholarly and theological concern. The term probably refers not to the Jewish people generally but to the Judaean authorities, and its polemical character reflects the painful separation of the Johannine community from the synagogue. Nevertheless, the Gospel’s rhetoric has had tragic consequences in the history of Christian anti-Judaism.

The relationship between the Fourth Gospel and the Beloved Disciple has been variously understood. The traditional identification with John the son of Zebedee has been questioned on the grounds that the Gospel’s theological sophistication and apparent late date are difficult to reconcile with a Galilean fisherman. Some scholars now regard the Beloved Disciple as a literary construct embodying the ideal witness, though the figure may well have a historical core.

The Sermon on the Mount’s antitheses (‘you have heard that it was said … but I say to you’) represent a remarkable claim to interpretive authority. By juxtaposing his own teaching with that of Sinai, Matthew’s Jesus assumes a role comparable to that of a new Moses, though the antithetical form goes beyond Mosaic typology toward a claim of sovereign authority over the Torah itself.

The Q source, reconstructed from material common to Matthew and Luke but absent from Mark, reveals a community’s understanding of Jesus that is distinct from the Markan tradition. Q’s Jesus is primarily a teacher of wisdom and a prophetic figure identified with Sophia; there is no passion narrative, suggesting that the Q community did not yet interpret Jesus’s death as the central saving event.

Recent scholarship has questioned the sharp dichotomy between Hellenistic and Jewish Christianity that dominated earlier reconstructions of Christian origins. The work of Martin Hengel and others has demonstrated that Palestinian Judaism was already significantly Hellenised by the first century, making it methodologically problematic to assign a motif to a ‘Hellenistic’ stage of development simply because it employs Greek concepts.

The Gospel of John’s extensive use of symbolism — light and darkness, water and wine, bread from heaven, the vine and the branches — creates a dense theological texture in which the material world becomes transparent to divine reality. This symbolic mode of discourse means that the Johannine miracles are ‘signs’ whose primary significance lies not in the wonders themselves but in what they reveal about Jesus’s identity.

The resurrection appearances in the Gospels exhibit a pattern of development that may reflect the early church’s evolving understanding. In the earlier traditions, appearances occur in Galilee; in later accounts, they are concentrated in Jerusalem. The movement from Galilee to Jerusalem may mirror the church’s own geographical and theological trajectory from its origins in the north to its establishment in the holy city.

Paul’s collection for the saints in Jerusalem, mentioned in Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, and Galatians, has been interpreted as more than a charitable enterprise. It may have functioned as a symbolic acknowledgment by the Gentile churches of their debt to the mother church, a tangible expression of the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers that Paul fought to maintain even as tensions threatened to divide them.

The concept of covenant is central to understanding the relationship between the Testaments in early Christian theology. The Epistle to the Hebrews develops the most systematic argument for the supersession of the Mosaic covenant by the new covenant in Christ, employing Platonic categories of shadow and reality to articulate what remains a thoroughly Jewish conviction: that Israel’s Scriptures find their telos in Jesus.

The role of meals in Jesus’s ministry has been analysed as a form of enacted parable. By eating with tax collectors and sinners, Jesus was not merely being sociable; he was performing the eschatological banquet in advance, enacting the inclusive character of the Kingdom and challenging the social boundaries that table fellowship normally reinforced.

The Gospel of Mark’s characterisation of the disciples as consistently failing to understand Jesus’s identity and mission has been interpreted as a pastoral strategy. If Mark was writing to a community experiencing persecution and failure, the disciples’ story would have functioned not as a negative example but as a source of reassurance: even those who walked with Jesus failed, yet were restored.

The relationship between Paul’s letters and the Acts account of his career raises significant historical problems. The discrepancies between the autobiographical data in Galatians and the narrative of Acts — particularly concerning Paul’s visits to Jerusalem — suggest that Luke had access to traditions about Paul but exercised considerable freedom in shaping them to fit his theological and literary programme.

The early Christian practice of baptism has been understood against several possible backgrounds: Jewish proselyte baptism, the washings of the Qumran community, and John’s baptism of repentance. The distinctively Christian innovation was linking baptism to the name of Jesus and interpreting it as participation in his death and resurrection. This Christological reframing transformed a rite of purification into a rite of incorporation.

The concept of the imperial cult provides essential context for understanding early Christian claims about Jesus’s lordship. When the New Testament declares ‘Jesus is Lord,’ it employs the same acclamation used for Caesar. The political subversiveness of this confession would have been apparent to ancient audiences, and the Apocalypse can be read as an extended counter-imperial polemic against the ideology of Roman power.

The ending of Mark at 16:8 (‘for they were afraid’) has generated extensive discussion. The grammatical awkwardness of the final sentence and the absence of resurrection appearances have led the majority of scholars to conclude that the original ending was lost or that Mark deliberately composed an open conclusion. Either possibility carries profound implications for how the Gospel’s message was designed to function.

The formation of the New Testament canon was a gradual and contested process rather than a single decision. Criteria of apostolicity, catholicity, and orthodoxy operated in complex ways, and the eventual exclusion of works such as the Shepherd of Hermas and the Apocalypse of Peter indicates that the boundaries remained fluid well into the fourth century. The canon as we now have it represents a negotiated consensus, not an inevitable outcome.

The Gospel of Luke’s concern with wealth and poverty has been the subject of diverse interpretations. Some readers find in Luke a programme of economic redistribution and a preferential option for the poor; others argue that Luke spiritualises poverty, redirecting the hope of the dispossessed toward eschatological reversal rather than material transformation. The tension between these readings is probably intrinsic to the text itself.

According to the consensus view among New Testament scholars, the Gospel of Mark was written around 70 CE, shortly before or after the destruction of the Jerusalem Temple. This dating is widely accepted based on internal and external evidence.

Most historians agree that Jesus of Nazareth was a historical figure who lived in first-century Palestine. The general scholarly consensus, based on multiple independent sources, is that he was baptised by John the Baptist and crucified under Pontius Pilate.

The Sadducees, as described by Josephus and the New Testament, were a Jewish sect that rejected the resurrection of the dead and held only the written Torah as authoritative. They were associated with the Temple priesthood.
The pool of Siloam was constructed in Jerusalem during the reign of King Hezekiah in the eighth century BCE. Archaeological excavations have confirmed its location and dimensions.

The Council of Jerusalem, described in Acts 15, was a meeting around 50 CE between Paul, Barnabas, and the Jerusalem church leaders. The council decided that Gentile converts were not required to be circumcised.
The term Pharisee refers to a Jewish sect active during the Second Temple period. The Pharisees emphasised oral tradition alongside the written Torah and believed in the resurrection of the dead.
The Acts of the Apostles follows the four Gospels in the New Testament canon. It narrates the spread of Christianity from Jerusalem to Rome and is traditionally attributed to Luke the Evangelist.
The Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem is venerated as the site of Jesus’s crucifixion and burial. The original church was constructed under Emperor Constantine in the fourth century CE.
The Epistle to the Galatians is one of the seven undisputed letters of Paul. It addresses a controversy in the Galatian churches regarding whether Gentile converts must observe the Mosaic law.
The Gospel of Luke opens with a formal preface addressed to Theophilus. The author states that he has carefully investigated the events and intends to provide an orderly account.
Bethlehem is located approximately ten kilometres south of Jerusalem in the Judaean hills. The Church of the Nativity, built in the fourth century, marks the traditional birthplace of Jesus.

The Epistle to the Hebrews is an anonymous letter in the New Testament. It presents Jesus as the ultimate high priest and draws extensively on Old Testament typology and the Levitical sacrificial system.
